units.translation: 397–414. Athene. The first question is how the goddess appears, whether really, as the scholiast on line 405 thinks, in a chariot. But 403 ⟦1⟧ proves as strongly as possible that she comes without a chariot, also not flying with wings, but striding through the air and thereby supported by the aegis as by a sail (cf. Introduction p. 15); so 405 must be explained metaphorically, if not emended. Now ⟦2⟧ is said quite similarly of the arriving messenger: ⟦3⟧; so if the feet are compared with the ends of the axle (indeed not without harshness), then here too the body together with the aegis can be designated as ⟦4⟧, and ⟦5⟧ can mean the legs. (Hermann, with Wakefield, corrects to ⟦6⟧: cf. above 372. ⟦7⟧ etc.; of course this is meant to recall ⟦8⟧; but one can also conversely be reminded of ⟦9⟧ by ⟦10⟧.) Another question is why the poet has the goddess come from the Troad, i.e. from Sigeion. A current interest for the Athenians, which the historically ill-informed scholiast has in mind, Sigeion did not have at that time at all; for after the Athenians had taken it from the Mytilenaeans in the 6th century, it was in any case reoccupied by Athens after the Persian Wars and was then, like Lemnos and Imbros, a tribute-paying allied city, E. Meyer, Geschichte des Altertums IV, § 394. So it is probably meant only to connect with the Trojan War, cf. 456 ff., 631 f., and the first play of the trilogy. As Athene then helped the father, so she now helps the son.
I came pursuing with untiring foot
in haste pursuing the guiding axle-ends of my feet

398 ⟦1⟧ occurs only here; the scholiast explains it with ⟦2⟧, Hesychius with ⟦3⟧ (manuscript ⟦4⟧)· ⟦5⟧, with which other glosses in him are to be compared: ⟦6⟧· ⟦7⟧ and ⟦8⟧· ⟦9⟧. The connection with ⟦10⟧ seems clear, but one can take offense at the meaning; for with this acquisition Athene then did not hurry in the least. So perhaps: securing my right as first acquirer.
properly, that which comes from prior occupation
399 ⟦1⟧ in a declarative sentence confirming or assuring, here about = "as is well known", cf. ⟦2⟧ 3 (Paley).
